subject: Archaeology
title: Archaeology and Indigenous Rights
description: A micro-lesson that makes Archaeology and Indigenous Rights usable.

hook.text: For a century, archaeologists dug up indigenous graves and stored skulls in drawers.

buildup.text: Thousands of Native American and Aboriginal remains were taken without consent.

discovery.text: NAGPRA and similar laws led to the reburial of thousands of ancestral remains.

twist.text: Scientists say reburial destroys data. Communities say ancestors deserve dignity.

climax.text: The best projects are now led by indigenous people who decide what to study.

punchline.text: They dug up the ancestors. The descendants said bring them home.

quiz.question: What shift is happening in indigenous archaeology?
options: Indigenous communities block all research on their lands
The best modern projects are led by indigenous communities

details.summary: Modern archaeology increasingly recognizes that indigenous communities have rights over ancestral sites, remains, and cultural knowledge. Laws like NAGPRA in the United States now require consultation with and return of remains to descendant communities, reshaping archaeological practice.
details.whyItMatters: For centuries, archaeologists excavated indigenous sites without consent and displayed remains in museums. The shift toward indigenous rights is transforming who controls the past and how archaeology is practiced globally.
takeaways: NAGPRA requires return of indigenous remains in the United States
Indigenous consultation is now standard in ethical archaeology
Descendant communities increasingly control their own heritage

faq.question: What is NAGPRA and how does it work?
faq.answer: The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (1990) requires US institutions to inventory indigenous human remains and sacred objects and return them to affiliated tribes. It established a legal framework for indigenous peoples to reclaim their ancestors and cultural patrimony.

faq.question: How has indigenous involvement changed archaeology?
faq.answer: Indigenous communities now co-direct excavations, approve research designs, and control publication of sensitive cultural knowledge. This collaboration produces better research because indigenous oral histories and traditional knowledge complement archaeological evidence.
